Philemon and Onesimus
fih-LEE-mon and oh-NES-ih-mus
proper noun phrase
Philemon: Greek Philēmōn, “loving”; Onesimus: Greek Onēsimos, “useful, profitable.” The master and runaway-slave-converted-to-Christ who are the subjects of Paul’s shortest extant epistle, the letter to Philemon (25 verses), one of the most pastorally rich documents in the NT.

📖 Biblical Definition

Philemon and Onesimus are the master-and-runaway-slave whose situation is the subject of Paul’s shortest extant epistle, the letter to Philemon (25 verses), one of the most pastorally rich documents in the New Testament. The historical situation reconstructed from the letter and the parallel reference in Colossians 4:9: Onesimus was a slave in the household of Philemon, a prominent member of the Colossian church; Onesimus had run away from his master (possibly after stealing from him—Phlm 18 suggests this) and somehow ended up with Paul in Rome (Paul was imprisoned, likely in Rome around AD 60-62); under Paul’s ministry, Onesimus was converted to Christ; Paul, recognizing both Onesimus’s legal obligation to return to his master and the new spiritual reality of his Christian brotherhood with Philemon, sent Onesimus back with this letter, appealing to Philemon to receive him not now as a slave but as a brother beloved. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, Paul’s diplomatic-apostolic approach. The letter is a masterpiece of tactful persuasion. Paul could have commanded Philemon’s acceptance of Onesimus on apostolic authority (Phlm 8: though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient); instead he beseeches Philemon for love’s sake (Phlm 9). He commends Philemon’s love and faith (Phlm 4-7); identifies himself as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ (Phlm 9); calls Onesimus my son... whom I have begotten in my bonds (Phlm 10); employs the wordplay on Onesimus’s name (which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me, Phlm 11—the Greek achrēston / euchrēston playing on Onesimus = useful); offers to pay any debt Onesimus owed (Phlm 18-19); even reminds Philemon that thou owest unto me even thine own self besides (Phlm 19, Philemon’s own conversion having come through Paul’s ministry). Second, the runaway-slave situation in Roman law. Under Roman law, a runaway slave was subject to severe punishment including death; the harboring of a runaway slave was itself a crime; the master’s right of severe discipline over the recovered slave was legally absolute. Paul’s request that Philemon receive Onesimus not as a slave but as a brother beloved (Phlm 16) was therefore not minor but radical, asking Philemon to override his absolute legal rights in favor of the gospel-realities of Christian brotherhood. Third, the transformative gospel-theology. The letter does not explicitly demand emancipation, but it lays out the principles from which the eventual Christian critique of slavery would develop: in Christ there is neither bond nor free (Gal 3:28); the slave is the Lord’s freeman, the freeman the Lord’s servant (1 Cor 7:22); Christian brotherhood transcends the slave-master distinction. Onesimus, the runaway slave, is now Philemon’s brother beloved; the gospel has overturned the social hierarchy in the realm where it operates (within the Christian family) without (in this letter) directly overturning the legal-social system as such. Fourth, Onesimus’s subsequent significance. Colossians 4:9 names Onesimus as one of the bearers of the Colossian letter, naming him a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. Onesimus has become a trusted Pauline messenger, an honored member of the Colossian church. (Later church tradition, possibly accurate, identified Onesimus as later becoming bishop of Ephesus—the runaway slave become Christian leader by the gospel’s transformative power.) The Philemon-Onesimus correspondence is therefore one of the most pastorally rich documents in the NT, illustrating the gospel’s power to transform legal-social relationships into substantive Christian brotherhood across the most rigid of ancient social barriers.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Philemon and Onesimus are the master and runaway-slave-converted-to-Christ who are the subjects of Paul’s shortest extant epistle, the letter to Philemon (25 verses); Paul’s appeal to Philemon to receive Onesimus not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved (Phlm 16) is one of the most pastorally rich illustrations of the gospel’s power to transform social relationships into substantive Christian brotherhood.

PHILEMON — A prominent member of the Colossian church, master of Onesimus, addressee of Paul’s shortest epistle.

ONESIMUS — Greek useful, profitable; runaway slave of Philemon converted to Christ under Paul’s ministry in Rome and sent back to his master with the letter to Philemon; subsequently a Pauline messenger and member of the Colossian church (Col 4:9).

📖 Key Scripture

Philemon 1:10-11 — "I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds: Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me."

Philemon 1:15-16 — "For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever; Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?"

Philemon 1:18-19 — "If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account; I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides."

Colossians 4:9 — "With Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They shall make known unto you all things which are done here."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Philemon-and-Onesimus letter is corrupted, on one side, by the liberation-theological reading that has criticized Paul for failing to demand explicit emancipation (against the letter’s actual revolutionary gospel-substance within its social-historical context)—and on the other by the historic-defensive reading (especially among American antebellum slaveholders) that used the letter’s return-of-Onesimus narrative as proof-text for the legitimacy of slavery itself, against the letter’s explicit brother-beloved transformation of the master-slave relationship.

expand to see more

The liberation-theological reading has criticized Paul for failing to demand explicit emancipation of Onesimus in the letter, treating the apparent acceptance of the slave-system as a moral failure of apostolic teaching. The critique misses the letter’s revolutionary gospel-substance within its social-historical context. In a Roman legal system where slavery was absolute and the runaway slave subject to severe punishment or death, Paul’s appeal to Philemon to receive Onesimus not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved was radically transformative. The letter does not abolish the legal slave-system (Paul could not have done so by apostolic command, and a frontal-attack approach would have likely produced massive backlash that the small church could not have survived); but it plants the gospel-principle from which the historic Christian critique of slavery developed—in Christ there is neither bond nor free; the slave is the Lord’s freeman; Christian brotherhood transcends the master-slave distinction. The recovery is the recovery of historical-contextual reading: the letter is not Paul’s acceptance of slavery but his strategic introduction of the gospel-principle that, faithfully applied across centuries, would dissolve the institution from within.

The opposite historic corruption is the defensive reading that, especially among American antebellum slaveholders, used the letter’s return-of-Onesimus narrative as proof-text for the legitimacy of slavery itself. The reading was sometimes accompanied by the broader misuse of Pauline-and-Petrine slave-master passages to argue for the divine sanction of the chattel-slavery institution. The misuse was profound and consequential, contributing to one of the gravest historical-moral failures of Christianity in modern history. Paul’s letter to Philemon, read in its full context, is precisely against the kind of slavery the antebellum South practiced: Paul instructs the master to receive the slave as a brother beloved, not to treat him as chattel property; the letter operates within the legal constraints of its day but plants the gospel-principle that overturns the institution’s moral foundation. Recover both ends. Refuse the liberation-theological critique that misses the letter’s revolutionary gospel-substance, and refuse the historic-defensive misuse that read the letter against its actual brother-beloved-transformation substance. The biblical Philemon-Onesimus letter is the pastorally-rich illustration of the gospel’s power to transform the most rigid of social-legal hierarchies into substantive Christian brotherhood within the realm where it operates.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Philēmōn (loving) and Onēsimos (useful, profitable); the master and runaway-slave-converted-to-Christ who are the subjects of Paul’s shortest extant epistle (25 verses); Paul’s appeal to Philemon to receive Onesimus not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved (Phlm 16); one of the most pastorally rich illustrations of the gospel’s power to transform social-legal hierarchies into substantive Christian brotherhood.

expand to see more

Greek Philēmōn (G5371) — Philemon (the singular NT use, the addressee of Paul’s epistle).

Greek Onēsimos (G3682) — Onesimus (2 NT uses: Phlm 10; Col 4:9).

Greek achrēstos / euchrēstos — useless / useful (the wordplay on Onesimus’s name in Phlm 11).

Greek doulos (G1401) — slave (the legal status Paul does not directly attack but transforms through gospel-brotherhood teaching).

Usage

"Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved—Paul’s revolutionary gospel-substance instruction transforming the master-slave relationship within Christ’s body."

"If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account—Paul’s personal assumption of any debt Onesimus owed, a vivid illustration of substitutionary-payment gospel-figure."
